paper_title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Adapting pretrained neural networks typically relies on optimizing model parameters using task-specific data, as exemplified by parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA [1]. Prior work has also demonstrated that model behavior can be altered through direct weight interventions, including knowledge editing [2, 3] and task-vector arithmetic [4]. Recently, Weight-Space Programming (WSP) has introduced different approach to model adaptation, enabling reasoning agents to inspect, interpret, and directly modify neural network parameters [5]. Rather than relying on gradient-based optimization or predefined editing procedures, WSP allows agents to diagnose model behavior, identify candidate computational mechanisms, and construct targeted weight modifications. This offers promising direction for adapting pretrained models without conventional fine-tuning, potentially reducing the dependence on large task-specific training datasets while enabling more deliberate interventions in the weight space. Early results demonstrate the potential of this approach. In the original WSP study, GPT-6 Astra improves the MATH-500 accuracy of Qwen3.5-0.8B from 7.9% to 48.1% by modifying only approximately 0.016% of its parameters, primarily addressing reasoning loops that prevent the model from completing its responses [5]. The resulting improvements also extend to instruction following, suggesting that localized interventions can affect behavior beyond their original target. However, the same study reports limited success when attempting to improve model without such identifiable failure modes. These observations raise fundamental question:To what extent can reasoning-driven weight interventions serve as general approach to model adaptation, rather than means of repairing specific behavioral failures? Despite these promising initial results, the effectiveness of WSP across diverse tasks, model scales, and independently executed editing processes remains insufficiently characterized. To address this question, we investigate WSP along three complementary dimensions. Capabilities: How effectively can WSP improve different model abilities, and how do the structure and scale of weight interventions relate to their outcomes? Generalization: Do improvements obtained through task-specific editing transfer to other capabilities without additional modifications, or do their effects remain confined to the target task? Limitations: How reliably can agents discover, validate, and select effective interventions, and how do editing outcomes vary across trajectories and model scales? These questions are particularly important because successful local modifications do not necessarily imply broader behavioral improvements, as also observed in prior studies of model editing and generalization [6]. In this work, we conduct systematic empirical investigation of WSP through 16 editing trajectories on Qwen3.50.8B and Qwen3.5-9B, covering seven benchmark families: MATH-500, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, GPQA Diamond, MedXpertQA, SciBench, and SciCode [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Our results reveal both the potential and the practical challenges of WSP. On full held-out evaluations, successful interventions achieve substantial improvements across multiple tasks, including 29.45-percentage-point gain on MATH-500 from modifying only 1,023 parameter values. We further find that Math-edited checkpoint transfers to GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, improving accuracy by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 percentage points, respectively, without further editing. However, intervention structures and outcomes vary considerably across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories ultimately retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these findings demonstrate that WSP can enable powerful and highly localized model adaptation, while highlighting the challenges of reliably discovering effective interventions and predicting their effects across tasks. As shown in Figure 1, WSP yield substantial held-out improvements across multiple benchmarks, particularly for the 0.8B model, while gains at the 9B scale are generally more modest.

sections.title: 2 Methods
sections.content: Pipeline Overview. We study Weight-Space Programming (WSP) as reasoning-driven approach to model adaptation, following the framework of Takehi et al. [5]. As illustrated in Figure 2, GPT-6 Astra serves as the 2 Figure 2 Overview of the WSP pipeline. reasoning agent analyzes model parameters, constructs weight interventions, and evaluates their effects using generation and teacher-forced observations. The selected checkpoint is subsequently evaluated against the original model on held-out data. editing agent, performing targeted weight-space interventions on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B [14]. The agent operates through persistent Python environment for weight analysis and modification, while model inference is performed by separate GPU worker. The original checkpoint remains unchanged throughout the editing process. Each search is allocated 50 successful forward-tool requests, enabling the agent to iteratively investigate model behavior, construct interventions, and evaluate candidate edits without access to gradients or backpropagation. Weight-Space Editing. iteration t, the agent constructs an update θt based on the current weights and accumulated observations Ht: Let θ0 denote the original model parameters and θt the current edited parameters. At θt+1 = bf16 (θt + θt) , θt = Et(θt, Ht), (1) where Et denotes the agent-generated editing program. Updates are computed in float32 and stored in bfloat16. Edits are restricted to admissible transformer-block parameters, while token embeddings, final normalization, the language-model head, and the model architecture remain fixed. The agent may construct arbitrary interventions within these constraints, including sparse MLP modifications, rank-one updates, attention-head rescaling, and combinations of these operations. All updates are computed directly from weights and observations rather than gradient-based optimization. Feedback and Evaluation. The agent evaluates candidate edits through two complementary modes: autoregressive generation, which measures task performance, and teacher forcing, which provides token log-probabilities and intermediate activations for mechanistic analysis. Based on development feedback, the agent selects final checkpoint, which is subsequently evaluated against the original model on held-out benchmarks under matched evaluation settings.

sections.title: 3.1 Benchmarks and Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate WSP on seven benchmarks covering math reasoning (MATH [7]), general knowledge (MMLU-Pro [8]), instruction following (IFEval [9]), scientific QA (GPQA Diamond [10]), medical QA (MedXpertQA [11]), scientific reasoning (SciBench [12]), and scientific coding (SciCode [13]). Table 1 summarizes the corresponding development data and held-out evaluation sets. Table 1 Benchmarks, task categories, and evaluation splits. Benchmark Task Type Development Data Held-out Test MATH MMLU-Pro IFEval GPQA Diamond MedXpertQA SciBench SciCode Math Reasoning General Knowledge Instruction Following Scientific QA Medical QA Scientific Reasoning Scientific Coding GSM8K/MATH train + AIME MMLU-Pro validation IFEval dev split GPQA Main MedQA English + MedXpertQA dev MedXpertQA-Text SciBench worked examples SciCode validation chains MATH-500 MMLU-Pro test IFEval test split GPQA Diamond SciBench test SciCode test chains We study Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B, reporting one editing trajectory for each modelbenchmark pair. For 0.8B MATH, the main tables report the column-507 editing trajectory; two further trajectories are analyzed separately. Each search begins from the original checkpoint and allows up to 50 forward-tool requests for generation and teacher-forced analysis. The agent selects its final checkpoint using development feedback alone, with the option of retaining the original weights. Evaluation follows benchmark-specific protocols. IFEval uses fixed 270/271 split of its 541 official prompts. SciBench employs numerical answer extraction with 5% relative tolerance, while SciCode evaluates complete executable code chains, separately from the conditional unit tests used during development. Further evaluation details are provided in the appendix.

sections.title: 3.2 Experimental Results
sections.content: Development and Held-out Performance. Table 2 summarizes the development and held-out results across 14 representative WSP editing trajectories, covering seven benchmarks and two model scales. For 0.8B Math, we report the single-column editing trajectory, with two additional independent searches analyzed separately. Across all seven benchmark categories, Qwen3.5-0.8B exhibits larger best-observed development gains than Qwen3.5-9B, with improvements reaching +43.75 percentage points on both Math and IFEval. On held-out evaluations, the 0.8B model achieves gains of +29.45, +4.42, +36.72, and +17.11 points on Math, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. The 9B model also improves on IFEval, SciBench, and SciCode, although with smaller gains. However, development improvements do not always translate into retained edits. In six trajectories, Astra ultimately selects the original checkpoint. Notably, the evaluated 9B Math candidate decreases held-out accuracy by 0.35 points, despite +29.69-point development gain. These results highlight the distinction between candidate discovery, held-out performance, and final checkpoint selection. 4 Table 2 Development and held-out performance across 14 representative WSP editing trajectories. sections.title: 3.3 Exploration Trajectory
sections.content: Figure 3 shows the complete 50-request exploration trajectory of the 0.8B MATH experiment, comprising 32 generation requests and 18 teacher-forced analyses. The agent progresses from behavioral diagnosis and component exploration to targeted interventions, controls, and broader validation. The trajectory illustrates how iterative feedback guides intervention discovery and selection. Figure 3 Exploration of the 0.8B MATH edit over 50 requests: development accuracy (top) and feedback modes (bottom).

sections.title: 3.4 Analysis of Weight-Space Interventions
sections.content: Weight-Space Interventions Generalize to Unseen Questions. Our results demonstrate that weight-space interventions can improve performance on previously unseen questions. Across three independent Math editing trajectories, Qwen3.5-0.8B achieves held-out gains of +29.45, +5.00, and +27.30 percentage points. Task-specific edits also improve GPQA Diamond (+4.42 pp), IFEval (+36.72 pp), and SciBench (+17.11 pp) on complete held-out evaluations  (Table 2)  . Together, these results establish that WSP improvements can extend beyond the development data used to construct the interventions. Editing Outcomes Vary Across Independent Searches. The three independent MATH searches exhibit substantial variation in their discovered interventions and held-out performance (Figure 4). Despite targeting the same model and benchmark, the primary search achieves +29.45 percentage-point improvement, while reruns 1 and 2 yield gains of +5.00 and +27.30 points, respectively. Although all three interventions modify the layer-23 MLP down-projection, they differ considerably in structure and parameter support. These results highlight the path-dependent nature of weight-space exploration, where different search trajectories can discover markedly different solutions within the same model. Figure 4 Three MATH searches yield distinct interventions and different held-out improvements on the same model. Intervention Structure Matters Beyond Scale. Figure 5 reveals striking contrast among three Math editing trajectories. Although all three interventions target the layer-23 MLP down-projection, they occupy three distinct regions of the parameter-scaleperformance space. The primary run modifies only 1,023 BF16 values in single output column, achieving the largest held-out improvement of +29.45 percentage points. In contrast, rerun 1 modifies 1,037,572 values through rank-one update but yields only +5.00 points, while rerun 2 changes 1,981,083 values and achieves +27.30 points. These contrasting outcomes demonstrate that the number of modified parameters alone does not predict editing effectiveness. Rather, intervention structure and the selection of computational targets play critical roles in determining downstream performance. 6 Figure 5 Parameter support, edit structure, and held-out gain across three layer-23 MLP interventions. Weight-Space Interventions Exhibit Cross-Task Transfer. To investigate cross-task generalization, we evaluate four task-edited checkpoints across additional benchmarks without further weight modifications, as shown in Figure 6. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, the Math-edited checkpoint achieves 28.28% on GPQA Diamond, 33.58% on IFEval, and 21.48% on SciBench. Conversely, the IFEval-edited checkpoint improves performance on Math and SciBench, reaching 21.40% and 3.28%, respectively. Cross-task effects are also observed at the 9B scale: the IFEval-edited checkpoint achieves 75.71% on SciBench, while the SciBench-edited checkpoint reaches 91.51% on IFEval. However, transfer is not uniformly beneficial, with some interventions producing marginal improvements or performance regressions on other tasks. These results demonstrate that weight-space interventions can influence capabilities beyond their original objectives, while the direction and magnitude of transfer depend on both the source intervention and the target task. Figure 6 Cross-task transfer of four task-edited checkpoints: 0.8B Math and IFEval (AB), and 9B IFEval and SciBench (CD). Dashed gray lines denote the base model; blue lines denote the transferred edited checkpoint. 7 Limited Search Budgets Constrain Weight Editing. Within the 50-request budget, Astra does not always identify sufficiently reliable weight intervention. For example, in 0.8B MedXpertQA, 9B GPQA Diamond, 9B MedXpertQA, and 9B MMLU-Pro, the agent ultimately retains the original weights despite observing positive development gains. For instance, the 9B GPQA search achieves an initial improvement of +6.25 percentage points, but subsequent validation shows slight performance decline. Similarly, the 9B MMLU-Pro search identifies promising candidates whose improvements diminish under broader evaluation. These outcomes highlight practical limitation of WSP: within fixed exploration budget, the agent may fail to discover and validate an intervention sufficiently effective to justify modifying the original model. Model Scale and Baseline Headroom Shape Editing Outcomes. Figure 7 reveals consistent contrast between baseline capability and observed editing gains across model scales. Qwen3.5-9B substantially outperforms Qwen3.5-0.8B before editing, particularly on MATH-500 (97.70% versus 8.35%) and SciBench (72.46% versus 1.38%). In contrast, the 0.8B model achieves larger best-observed development gains across all seven benchmark categories. This pattern highlights the role of initial model capability and available improvement headroom in weight-space editing. The results suggest that smaller models offer greater opportunities for measurable improvements, while stronger models present more constrained search landscape. Figure 7 Baseline accuracy and best-observed development gains for Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B.

sections.title: 4 Discussion
sections.content: Our systematic evaluation reveals both the potential and limitations of Weight-Space Programming. Across diverse tasks and model scales, WSP achieves substantial held-out improvements and exhibits asymmetric cross-task transfer, with both beneficial and adverse effects. Independent editing trajectories further show that effectiveness depends not only on the number of modified parameters, but also on intervention structure, computational targets, and exploration paths. However, development gains do not always translate into reliable held-out improvements, and repeated evaluations incur substantial computational costs. The mechanisms governing successful editing and generalization remain unclear, including the effects of jointly modifying multiple parameter locations and the influence of development data size and diversity. Moreover, WSP has yet to be systematically evaluated on longer-horizon reasoning and complex agentic tasks. These findings highlight the need for more reliable intervention selection, efficient evaluation, and deeper mechanistic understanding.

sections.title: A Supplementary Experimental Protocol
sections.content: Each search pairs an editor model, GPT-6 Astra at maximum reasoning effort, with target model, Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-9B. The editor observes the target only through forward requests, with budget of 50 successful requests per search. It may also run up to 300 Python analyses per search to inspect weights, analyze returned observations, and compute edits. These analyses do not run inference on the target model. There are two request types, and each successful request of either type counts once against the budget. generation request (G) samples answers from the target and returns them with task scores when the items come from graded set. teacher-forced request (TF) scores continuations supplied by the editor, returning conditional logprobabilities and any requested activations. TF requests yield no task accuracy. The editor chooses the questions, batch size, number of samples, token cap, and weight states for each request, and it may adapt these choices to earlier observations. One request can therefore contain many prompts and samples, as well as both the original and the edited weights. Editing is gradient-free and acts directly on parameters. The editor uses no backward passes, no optimizers, and no iterative loss fitting. Edits are computed in float32 and written to the BF16 checkpoint. Because of this, the number of values an editor targets can be larger than the number of stored values that actually change. Table 3 lists the settings shared by all searches. The Math Primary and Math Rerun 2 searches used broad ability-improvement objective from the start. Math Rerun 1 began with loop-focused objective that was broadened after 46 successful requests. The GPQA and MedXpertQA objectives were broadened after 27 and 26 requests, respectively. These independent trajectories vary in prompt history and in the editors adaptive experimental choices. Table 3 Essential search and decoding settings shared across searches.

sections.title: F Prompt
sections.content: This appendix reproduces the initial editor prompt as parameterized template from the frozen runtime. Anglebracketed fields substitute the model name and architecture, the held-out evaluation and scoring contract, the development-data description and task-specific tool contract, the CPU memory bound, and number of layers. Paths use /model, /practice, and /work. Table 4 lists benchmark data and scoring. Shared instructions direct the editor to improve capabilities, diagnose failures from the current experiments evidence, test interventions causally, and confirm accuracy on fresh development questions. TASK. You are given the weights of language model, <MODEL_NAME_AND_ARCHITECTURE>. Your job is to improve its capabilities by EDITING ITS WEIGHTS DIRECTLY: find out what goes wrong inside the network when it fails at the target tasks and repair that with targeted changes. HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED. <HELDOUT_BENCHMARK_AND_COVERAGE>. <TEST_SAMPLES_PER_ITEM> samples per item, separately for original and edited weights. You never see this test set. Metric: <TASK_METRIC>. Prompt protocol: <TASK_PROMPT_PROTOCOL>. The chat template has thinking enabled. Sampling is temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, presence penalty 1.5 and at most 32768 new tokens. Final sampling uses seed 0 for each prompt on both models. Config, tokenizer and decoding are fixed; only weight values can change. This is new independent experiment with no previous edits, notes, trajectories or published editing recipe. WHAT COUNTS. We want edits that come from understanding the network: find out what goes wrong when it fails at the target tasks, identify the components responsible (specific neurons, heads, directions or circuits) and change them in way you can justify with evidence. Any specific, evidence-supported failure mechanism is in scope. The objective is improved correctness on unseen problems. Possible failure categories include incorrect knowledge retrieval, calculation or logical inference, misunderstanding constraints, answer selection or expression, and failure to complete useful response. These are examples, not required diagnosis or an exhaustive list. Select mechanisms using this experiment's practice data; no failure category or component is preferred in advance. Out of scope, and refused by save_edit: the final norm (model.language_model.norm.weight), the input embedding / output layer (model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight, lm_head.weight), and any edit that only multiplies whole tensor by constant. Global knobs (making the whole output distribution sharper or flatter) are not what we are looking for, and neither is making the model skip its thinking or close it early regardless of the problem; repairing any specific, causally supported failure within these rules is in scope. WHAT YOU HAVE. 1. persistent Python kernel (no internet, no GPU): variables survive between your code blocks, like notebook. The model's files are read-only in /model, practice problems read-only in /practice, and /work is your read-write folder. Available: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU), pandas, sympy, networkx, safetensors, tokenizers. Defined in advance: NAMES (all tensor names), load(name) (a float32 torch tensor: your current edit if there is one, else the original), load_original(name), save_edit(name, tensor), drop_edit(name), edited() and tok (the tokenizer). Gradients are disabled. To run code, reply with exactly one block that starts with ```python and nothing else; if its last line is an expression, its value is shown. One execution may take up to 900 seconds; the CPU controller has total memory limit of <CPU_MEMORY_GIB> GiB; output is cut at 10,000 characters. You may run code up to 300 times. If the kernel is restarted (time or memory limit), its variables are lost and you are told so. 2. <DEVELOPMENT_DATA_AND_TASK_SPECIFIC_CONTRACT> Development questions are disjoint from the held-out test after normalized text matching. You may partition development questions for your own confirmation, but no such partition is hidden test. 3. forward-pass tool with budget of 50 forward passes in total. forward pass is one of two things, and each counts as one pass: (a) GENERATION: the model answers up to 512 generations (problems samples) with the evaluation's protocol (thinking enabled, the same sampling); custom prompts are used verbatim without an appended math instruction. Reply with exactly one block that starts with ```forward and contains JSON: {"type": "generate", "model": "original", "edited" or "both", "problems": ["<practice id>", ...], "prompts": ["<your own user message>", ...] (optional), "n": samples per item (items <= 512; with "both" <= 256 per model), "max_tokens": at most 32768, "activations": {"layers": [layer indices 0..<NUM_LAYERS>], "mlp": true or false} (optional)} "original" runs the unedited weights, "edited" your current edits, and "both" runs both on the same items and returns paired comparison (the accuracy difference edited - original over items with its standard error, and how many samples went from wrong to right and back). The sampling seed of every item is fixed by the problem, in every pass and for both models (this makes the two models' answers to problem largely share their random numbers, though long answers drift apart once token differs). Every answer to practice problem is graded. You get the accuracy (overall and by source), the mean length, the share cut at max_tokens and the failure counts; texts, extracted answers and grades are in /work/gen_<k>.jsonl (with "both": /work/gen_<k>_original.jsonl and /work/gen_<k>_edited.jsonl). With "activations", for every generated answer the model's residual stream at the requested layers (0 = embeddings, = after layer l) is saved, taken at the last token of the prompt and averaged over the answer's first 8,192 tokens (and the MLPs' down_proj inputs with "mlp": true), with each answer's grade: /work/gen_<k>_acts/ (index.json lists the files and samples; with "both" one folder per model). (b) TEACHER-FORCED: the model reads up to 1,024 texts of up to 32,768 tokens each, at most 524,288 tokens in total (no generation; it takes seconds to few minutes). Reply with ```forward block containing JSON: {"type": "teacher_forced", "model": "original" or "edited", "texts": ["raw text", ...] or "chats": [[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}], ...] (add "enable_thinking": true for the thinking template), "return": {"token_logprobs": true, "topk": (at most 50), "hidden_states": [layers 0..<NUM_LAYERS>], "mlp_act": [layers], "attn_layers": [full-attention layers only; at most 2 texts of at most 2,048 tokens]}} The results of (b) are .npy files (with meta.json) in /work/fwd_<k>/, right-padded to the longest text (at most 6 GB per pass). request that fails does not count against the budget. generation pass takes up to about half an hour at full size (answers can be 32,768 tokens long). HOW TO WORK. 1. Diagnose first. Compare correct and incorrect practice responses, including completed wrong answers, missing answers and token-limit truncations. Separate observable symptoms from proposed causes; long or truncated response is not automatically evidence of repetition. Use representative examples and available references to identify distinct failure mechanisms and assess their frequency, relevance to accuracy and causal testability. Consider competing explanations before 20 committing the remaining budget. Repetition is one possible mechanism to test if the evidence supports it; it is neither required nor the default diagnosis. Choose what to investigate from this run's own evidence. 2. Localize causally. That component is more active on correct answers is not enough (correct answers come from easier and shorter problems). Before relying on component, show that changing it changes the behaviour you predicted, and try several strengths to see dose-response. 3. Measure with enough power. Accuracy over generations has standard error of about 50/sqrt(n) percentage points: about 4.4 points at 128 generations, 2.2 at 512. Compare original and edited weights on the SAME problems: generation pass with "model": "both" does this with the same random seeds and reports the paired difference with its standard error, which is usually much smaller than that of two separate measurements; do not compare with an accuracy measured on other problems. Keep an edit only if its gain is clearly larger than its standard error on problems that were not used to choose it. lower share of cut-off answers does not by itself mean more correct answers: judge edits by accuracy. Dense measurements help too and are cheap: one teacher-forced pass can read the reference solutions of up to 1,024 practice problems (or the model's own good versus failing continuations) and gives signal on every token. Select edit strengths from measured causal effects; small and large changes are both admissible, and neither is preferred in advance. 4. Plan your forward passes (see the budget above): for example one diagnostic generation with activations, teacher-forced passes for dense paired measurements, and final paired generation ("model": "both") on problems you have not used to confirm. 5. Work efficiently: state the hypothesis of each code block in its first comment line; work through the model in parts; load things once into kernel variables; print compact summaries, never whole arrays (and never raw lists of vocabulary tokens: the vocabulary contains offensive and adult strings and printing them can get the session refused by the provider's content filter; print digits, math symbols, common math words or token ids instead; outputs are shown in ASCII only, other characters appear as '?'; likewise print short excerpts of generated texts, at most about 300 characters each, not whole transcripts); keep /work/notes.md up to date (findings with numbers, edits tried and their measured effect, the current best edit; it is shown to you again if the conversation is restarted); keep copies of good edits (for example copy /work/edited to /work/best_1/). RULES. Not allowed: (a) gradient descent or any other training: no backward passes, autograd or optimizers, and no iterative fitting of weights to loss; (b) running the model other than through the forward-pass tool: do not implement or simulate the network's computation on any input in the kernel; (c) internet access or search (there is none). Allowed: any analysis of the weights and of forward-pass results, any use of the practice problems, and any direct edit of the weights that you compute and that is in scope. HOW THE SESSION RUNS. It continues until all 50 forward passes are used (replying without code block does not end it earlier); after that, make your final choice (the tensors in /work/edited when you finish are submitted) and reply without code block, saying what you changed, the evidence for it and why you expect it to help.
